flashcards.definition: The OSI layer that delivers frames within one local segment by MAC address and has no concept of separate networks; forwarding at this layer is called switching.

reference.title: Layer 2 vs Layer 3 Addressing and Forwarding

flashcards.definition: The OSI layer where IP gives logical addressing and packets are forwarded between subnets, which is called routing; routers at this layer set the edges of broadcast domains.

reference.title: Layer 2 vs Layer 3 Addressing and Forwarding

flashcards.definition: Runs directly on IP to report errors and send status messages about packet delivery; ping sends its request packets to test connectivity.
Runs directly on IP to tunnel packets across an intermediate network through virtual point-to-point links, as some VPNs do; it can carry IPv4 and IPv6 over IPv4.
Traffic sent to a single recipient, using an address that identifies just that one network interface.
Traffic sent to a subnet's last address (all host bits set to 1), so every host in the subnet receives it; routers normally do not forward it, and IPv6 has none.
Traffic from one host delivered only to the hosts that joined its group, using an address from a reserved range; IPv6 uses it in place of broadcast.
Traffic to a group of hosts that share one unicast address, which routers deliver to just the closest one; it has no address range of its own.
An IPv4 address that can reach other networks and hosts over the Internet, allocated through regional registries and ISPs, unlike the ranges set aside for private use.

The address ranges that are not routable over the Internet and that any organization can use without applying: 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, and 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255.
The reserved 127.0.0.0/8 range, typically 127.0.0.1, used to check that TCP/IP is installed on the computer itself; packets sent to it are not processed by a network adapter.
Dividing one IP network into smaller layer 3 broadcast domains with fewer hosts each, by moving bits from the host portion of the address into the mask.
Gives the subnets inside one IP network different prefix lengths, so each fits its number of hosts instead of all being the same size; designs usually start with the largest.
Uses bits normally in the network ID to summarize several contiguous networks as one shorter prefix (supernetting), so outside routers need only one routing table entry.
The IPv4 address class whose first octet is 1 to 126, with a default mask of 255.0.0.0 (/8).
The IPv4 address class whose first octet is 128 to 191, with a default mask of 255.255.0.0 (/16).
The IPv4 address class whose first octet is 192 to 223, with a default mask of 255.255.255.0 (/24).
The IPv4 address class from 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255, used for multicasting.
The IPv4 address class from 240.0.0.0 through 255.255.255.255, reserved for experimental use and testing.
The 128-bit addressing scheme designed to mitigate IPv4 address exhaustion; an address is eight 16-bit blocks of hex, and :: can replace one run of zero blocks, only once in an address.
Inserting IPv6 packets into IPv4 packets to carry them across an IPv4 network, as 6to4, Teredo, and GRE do; it has high overhead and is less efficient than dual stack.
Hosts and routers run IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time, so they can communicate with devices that have either type of address; most try IPv6 first.
Lets an IPv6 host reach an IPv4 host through a gateway router that translates: the router strips a special prefix from the destination and forwards the packet with IPv4 headers.
A host can reach hosts on its own subnet but not remote ones, because the router address it sends remote traffic to is wrong.
A host whose address is not a valid host address in its neighbors' subnet, such as one from another subnet; it is unlikely to communicate on the network at all.
Two systems configured with the same address, from two static settings or a static one inside a DHCP scope; Windows detects it and shows a warning.

reference.title: Duplicate IP and MAC Address Issues

flashcards.definition: A host's prefix is longer or shorter than its neighbors': too long, and it sends replies to local hosts through the router; too short, and it cannot reach a remote subnet it thinks is local.
Sends ICMP request packets to a host to test basic connectivity and round-trip time, on Windows and Linux; on Windows, -t keeps it sending until it is stopped.
The Windows command that shows each interface's IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway; /release gives up a DHCP address, and /renew renews the lease.
The legacy Linux command, deprecated on most modern distributions, that can still safely be used to report each adapter's address settings.
The current Linux command that replaced the legacy tools; it reports and changes interface addresses and routes, but its changes are not persistent unless run from a startup script.
Views and edits the cache of IP-to-MAC mappings a host has recently learned: -a lists it, -s adds an entry, and -d deletes entries (-d * clears them all).
The 32-bit value whose contiguous 1s mark the network ID bits of an IPv4 address, revealed by ANDing the two; it is written in dotted decimal or as a slash prefix that counts its 1s.
The host setting that gives the address of a local router with a path to remote networks; the host sends it every packet bound for a different network or subnet.
The part of an IPv4 address that identifies a single device within its network; it is the bits the mask sets to 0, so 32 minus the prefix length.
Finds the MAC address that goes with an IPv4 address on the local subnet using broadcast requests; for a remote destination, it finds the default gateway's MAC address.
Runs directly on IP, with no TCP or UDP, to configure multicast group memberships so hosts can join a group and receive its traffic.
Two interfaces with the same hardware address both answer ARP queries, so traffic is split between them or reaches only one; it can be a sign of spoofing.

reference.title: Duplicate IP and MAC Address Issues

flashcards.definition: The fe80::/10 address that spans only a single subnet, since routers do not forward it; APIPA is the IPv4 equivalent, but a host always has one, even with a global address.
Builds a 64-bit IPv6 interface ID from a 48-bit MAC address by inserting fffe in the middle and flipping the 7th bit (the U/L bit) of the first byte.
Automatic tunneling of IPv6 packets across an IPv4 network that needs no host configuration; its addresses use the 2002::/16 prefix.
The tunneling protocol Windows hosts use to carry IPv6 packets as UDP messages over IPv4; it needs compatible clients and servers.
A switch capability that delivers multicast frames only to the group's members; a switch without it floods them out of every port like a broadcast.
The layer 3 protocol that provides logical network addressing and forwarding; its datagrams, or packets, carry payloads such as TCP segments, UDP datagrams, and ICMP messages.
